segments.translation: Through the realization of all [dharmas]{dharma}, [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha} sets forth that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as Sarahapāda setting forth ‘that same meaning’ (presumably that of the preceding song) through the realization of all [dharmas]{dharma} (cp.22.m1). The Tibetan makes the realization an epithet of the poet: ‘Sarahapāda, who has understood all phenomena’ (chos thams cad khong du chud pa'i sa ra ha'i zhabs).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has don de nyid chos thams cad khong du chud pa'i sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis gsungs te, ‘Sarahapāda, who has understood all phenomena, spoke that very meaning’, making sarvadharmādhigama an epithet of the poet. The Sanskrit instrumental sarvadharmādhigamena is translated as the means: ‘through the realization of all dharmas’.

tam evārtham, ‘that same meaning’, points back without saying to what; Munidatta uses the phrase to link a song to what precedes it. The note hedges (‘presumably that of the preceding song’); the reviewer may prefer to drop the gloss.

segments.translit: apaṇetyādi | anādyavidyāvāsanādoṣeṇa bhavanirvvāṇakalpāropaṇaṃ caritvā loko 'yaṃ bhrāntyā svayam eva bhavabandhanabaddho bhavatīti |
segments.translation: ‘By themselves’ and the rest. Through the fault of the [habitual tendencies]{vasana} of beginningless [ignorance]{avidya}, these people, having engaged in the conceptual [imputation]{aropa} of [existence and nirvāṇa]{bhava-nirvana}, in [confusion]{bhranti} become bound by themselves with the [bond]{bandhana} of [existence]{bhava}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as self-bondage: through the habitual tendencies of beginningless [ignorance]{avidya}, people impute the concepts ‘existence’ and ‘nirvāṇa’, and so, in [confusion]{bhranti}, bind themselves in existence (cp.22.m2). The Tibetan instead has them wander in this world ('jig rten 'dir 'khyam) and both bind and free themselves in existence.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ends rang nyid kyis srid par 'ching ba dang grol bar byed pa'i phyir ro, ‘because they themselves bind and free [themselves] in existence’. The Sanskrit has only binding (bhavabandhanabaddho bhavati); ‘and free’ has no counterpart in it. Mentioned in the note because it changes the point.

Where the Sanskrit has loko 'yaṃ bhrāntyā, ‘these people, in confusion’, the Tibetan has 'jig rten 'dir 'khyam zhing, ‘wandering in this world’: it apparently took bhrānti in the root sense of bhram-, ‘roam’ (the glossary lists 'khyam among the Tibetan forms for bhrānti), and loka as ‘world’. The Sanskrit is followed; ‘these people’ matches the draft’s ‘people’ for the song’s loa.

bhavanirvāṇakalpāropaṇaṃ caritvā: literally ‘having carried out the imputation of concepts (kalpa) of existence and nirvāṇa’; rendered ‘having engaged in the conceptual imputation of existence and nirvāṇa’. The Tibetan has rtog par sgro btags shing byas pa, ‘imputed as concepts and made’. caritvā could also be ‘having gone about in’.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena svajñānaṃ dṛḍhayati (dṛḍhayanti) —
ahma ityādi | siddhācāryyasarahapādā evaṃ vadanti[ti] | gurucaraṇareṇuprasādāt bhāvasvarūpaparijñānenācintyā yogino vayaṃ | ata eva utpādādibhaṅgaṃ kīdṛśaṃ bhavatīti na jānīmaḥ |
tathā ca ekaślokā bha(bhava)gavatī —
utpādasthitibhaṅgadoṣarahitām ityādi ||
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes his own knowledge firm: ‘We…’ and the rest. The [siddha]{siddha} master [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha} speaks thus: ‘Through the [grace]{prasada} of the dust of the [guru]{guru}'s feet, by fully knowing the [true nature]{svarupa} of things, we are [inconceivable]{acintya} [yogis]{yogi}. That is why we do not know what [arising]{utpada} and so on through perishing are like.’ And so the [Ekaślokā Bhagavatī]{tx-ekaslokabhagavati}: ‘Her, free of the faults of arising, abiding and perishing…’ and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the refrain as Saraha making his own knowledge firm: by the grace of the guru's feet he knows the true nature of things, so ‘we are [inconceivable]{acintya} yogis’ who do not know what arising and the rest are like (cp.22.m3). The Tibetan lacks ‘we do not know’, apparently referring the line to worldly people.

citations.quoted: utpādasthitibhaṅgadoṣarahitām ityādi (‘Her, free of the faults of arising, abiding and perishing…’ and so on)
citations.work: Ekaślokā Bhagavatī (so Munidatta names it; not otherwise identified)

flags.note: For ata eva utpādādibhaṅgaṃ kīdṛśaṃ bhavatīti na jānīmaḥ, ‘that is why we do not know what arising and so on through perishing are like’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de'i phyir skye dang zhes bya ba la sogs pas 'jig rten pa ji lta ba bzhin du gyur pa zhes pa'o: it cites ‘birth and…’ (line 2b) and says it means ‘as it has come to be for worldly people’. It has no ‘we do not know’. The Sanskrit is followed; the Tibetan seems to rest on a different reading.

Smaller Tibetan differences: singular bdag nyid, ‘I myself’, for vayam, ‘we’; bla ma'i zhabs kyi drin, ‘the kindness of the guru's feet’, without ‘dust’ (reṇu); and the source taken as tshigs su bcad pa gcig gis bcom ldan 'das ma la, ‘with one verse, to the Blessed Lady’, rather than as a title.

utpādādibhaṅga is literally ‘arising-etc.-perishing’; the ādi presumably covers abiding (sthiti), which the quoted verse names. Rendered ‘arising and so on through perishing’ rather than supplying ‘abiding’.

Shastri prints dṛḍhayati(nti), suggesting the honorific plural dṛḍhayanti (as with vadanti); vadanti[ti] has a restored syllable; bha(bhava)gavatī carries the edition’s parenthesis, and Bhagavatī is read. None changes the sense. The lemma ahma differs in spelling from the song text’s ambhe.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena utpādasvarūpam āhuḥ —
jaiso ityādi | sarvve nairātmāvagamena kasyotpādo vidyate | bho yogīndrāḥ | svayam eva ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya vadanti | yasyotpādo nāsti tasya bhaṅgo 'pi na dṛśyate |
tathā cādvayasiddhau —
yasya svabhāvo notpattir vināśo naiva dṛśyate |
taj jñānam advayaṃ nāma sarvvasaṃkalpavarjjitam ||
ata eva jīva(vi)tā puruṣeṇa sambhavāhavena saha bhedopalambho (°mbhe) nāstīti |
tathā ca sūtake —
suptaprabuddhe tu na cānyabhedaḥ
saṃkalpayet svapnaphalābhilāṣī |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [arising]{utpada}: ‘As…’ and the rest. Through understanding the [selflessness]{nairatmya} of all, whose arising is there, O [lords of yogis]{yogindra}? He says this addressing himself. What has no arising, of that no perishing is seen either. And so in the [Advayasiddhi]{tx-advayasiddhi}: ‘That whose own [nature]{svabhava} is no arising, and whose destruction is not seen at all, is the knowledge called [nondual]{advaya}, free of all [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}.’ That is why no difference is apprehended between the [living]{jivanta} person and the [dead]{mrta}. And so in the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}: ‘Between sleeping and waking there is no other difference; one who longs for the fruit of [dreams]{svapna} would imagine one.’
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet the nature of arising. Addressing himself as ‘lords of yogis’, Saraha asks whose arising there is once the [selflessness]{nairatmya} of all is understood; what does not arise is not seen to perish, so living and dead are not apprehended as different (cp.22.m4), citing the Advayasiddhi on nondual knowledge and the Sūtaka on sleep and waking.

citations.quoted: yasya svabhāvo notpattir vināśo naiva dṛśyate | taj jñānam advayaṃ nāma sarvasaṃkalpavarjitam (‘That whose own nature is no arising, and whose destruction is not seen at all, is the knowledge called nondual, free of all conceptual thought.’)
suptaprabuddhe tu na cānyabhedaḥ saṃkalpayet svapnaphalābhilāṣī (‘Between sleeping and waking there is no other difference; one who longs for the fruit of dreams would imagine one.’)

flags.note: sambhavāhavena is obscure and probably corrupt (sambhava, ‘coming into being’ + āhava, ‘battle, summons’?). It is rendered ‘the dead’ because the song line pairs the living with the dead (maalem̐) and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has skyes bu gson pa dang shi ba dag la, ‘between a living and a dead person’. A reading such as saṃbhavābhāvena, ‘one without coming-into-being’, is a guess. Also: jīva(vi)tā is the printed jīvatā with Shastri’s jīvitā (both ‘living’); for bhedopalambho(mbhe) the nominative is kept.

The printed sarvve nairātmavagamena is read as one compound, sarva-nairātm(y)āvagamena, ‘through understanding the selflessness of all’, with the Tibetan thams cad bdag med par khong du chud pas, ‘through understanding everything as selfless’. As printed, sarve would be a nominative plural with nothing to agree with.

The Tibetan comment’s lemma, gang 'dir, is the opening of couplet 4 (4a) in the Tibetan song, not of couplet 3 (ji ltar…); the Sanskrit lemma jaiso is couplet 3. The Tibetan also renders bhaṅga, ‘perishing’, as 'chi ba, ‘death’ (gang la skye ba med pa de la 'chi ba yang ma mthong), matching the song’s birth and death, and has rmi lam, ‘dream’, for supta, ‘sleeping’, in the Sūtaka verse.

Sūtaka verse: suptaprabuddhe tu na cānyabhedaḥ is taken as ‘between sleeping and waking there is no other difference’; the object of saṃkalpayet (‘would imagine’) is supplied as ‘one’ (a difference). The Tibetan reads rnam par rtog byed rmi lam 'bras bu mngon 'dod can, ‘one who conceptualizes is one who longs for the fruit of dreams’. The two half-lines may belong to a longer verse.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena svayam evānuśaṃsām āhuḥ —
yasmin maraṇādibhayaṃ vā vidyate | so 'pi yogī rasāyane vividhādikalpaprayogaṃ karoti | vayaṃ punaḥ maraṇādibhaye niḥśaṅkanirvvikalparūpāḥ |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he himself speaks [praise]{anusamsa}. Anyone in whom there is fear of [death]{marana} and the like: that [yogi]{yogi} too applies procedures of various kinds and the like in [alchemy]{rasayana}. We, however, are without doubt and without [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} in the face of the fear of death and the like.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet praise spoken by Saraha himself: a yogi who fears death and the like busies himself with the various procedures of [alchemy]{rasayana}, but ‘we’ are without doubt or conceptual thought about the fear of death (cp.22.m5). The Tibetan makes those procedures ‘gold-making and the like’ (gser 'gyur la sogs pa).

flags.note: vividhādikalpaprayoga is awkward (‘the application of various-etc. procedures’); rendered ‘applies procedures of various kinds and the like’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gser 'gyur la sogs pa sna tshogs pa'i cho ga rab tu sbyor bar byed, ‘applies various rites such as gold-making’.

The Tibetan has the singular bdag, ‘I’, for vayam, takes punaḥ as ‘again’ (slar yang) rather than ‘however’, and fuses the two adjectives as ‘without the conceptual thought of doubt’ (the tshom gyi rnam par rtog pa med pa) where the Sanskrit has niḥśaṅkanirvikalpa, ‘without doubt and without conceptual thought’. Neither the Sanskrit nor the Tibetan cites a lemma here.
The vā in maraṇādibhayaṃ vā is taken as emphatic (‘any’), since there is no second alternative; the Tibetan has 'ang, ‘also, even’.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena punar apy anuśaṃsām āhuḥ —
ye ye ityādi | ye ye bālayoginaḥ | jambūdvīpamahāsthāne sacarācare bhramanti | athavā mantrauṣadhyādiśaktyā tridaśaṃ devālayaṃ gacchanti (gacchati) | te 'pi gurumārgālabdhatvād amaratvaṃ na prāpnuvanti | vayam apy acchedyābhedyarūpā[ḥ] |
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks [praise]{anusamsa} once more: ‘Those who…’ and the rest. Whatever [novice yogins]{balayogin} wander among [the moving and the unmoving]{sacaracara} in the great places of [Jambudvīpa]{pl-jambudvipa}, or by the power of [mantras]{mantra}, herbs and the like go to [the Thirty]{tridasa}, the abode of the gods: they too do not attain [deathlessness]{amaratva}, because they have not gained the [guru]{guru}'s [path]{marga}. We, however, are of a form that cannot be cut or broken.
segments.note: Munidatta reads this as further praise: novice yogins who wander in the great places of Jambudvīpa, or reach the gods' heaven by mantras and herbs, do not attain [deathlessness]{amaratva}, lacking the guru's path; ‘we’ cannot be cut or broken (cp.22.m6). The Tibetan has ‘having gained the guru's path’ (bla ma'i lam thob nas), without the negative.

flags.note: For gurumārgālabdhatvāt, ‘because they have not gained the guru's path’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de yang bla ma'i lam thob nas 'chi ba med pa nyid thob pa ma yin no, ‘they too, having gained the guru's path, do not attain deathlessness’, as if reading gurumārgalabdhatvāt without the negative a-. That contradicts the Sanskrit and makes little sense in context; the Sanskrit is followed, and the note records the difference.

Munidatta’s paraphrase puts tridaśaṃ devālayam, ‘the Thirty, the abode of the gods’, where the song has tiasa; the Tibetan comment has sum cu rtsa gsum gyi gnas, ‘the abode of the Thirty-three’, while the Tibetan song line has no equivalent of tiasa. This is a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss, so it is not listed under equations.

jambūdvīpamahāsthāne: ‘in the great places of Jambudvīpa’ (singular in form, perhaps collective). mahāsthāna may mean the great sacred sites (pīṭha) frequented by tantric yogis; the Tibetan has gnas chen po, the usual word for such sites. ‘Great places’ keeps it open.

The lemma reads ye ye, ‘whoever’, where the song has a single je (the Tibetan lemma gang gi follows its own song line). Shastri’s gacchanti(ti) suggests the singular gacchati; the plural is kept to agree with ye ye bālayoginaḥ. Smaller Tibetan differences: singular bdag, ‘I’, for vayam, and gzhig tu med pa, ‘cannot be destroyed’, for abhedya.

segments.translit:
pañca[ma]padena vartma(tmā)māhātmyam āhuḥ —
jāmetyādi | karttṛkarmmavihīnasya yogīndrasya janmanā karmma kiṃ bhavati | karmmaṇā vā utpādaś ca | ata eva sarahapādāḥ svābhiprāyaṃ vadanti | paramārthavid yogināṃ acintyo hi |
segments.translation: With the fifth [verse]{pada} he states the greatness of the [path]{marga}: ‘From [birth]{janma}…’ and the rest. For the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, who is free of agent and [action]{karma}, does action come about through birth? Or [arising]{utpada} through action? That is why [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha} states his own intention: for [yogis]{yogi} who know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, it is indeed [inconceivable]{acintya}.
segments.note: Munidatta calls the last couplet the greatness of the path. Of the lord of yogis, free of agent and action, he asks whether action comes from birth or arising from action; so Saraha states his view: for yogis who know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, it is inconceivable (cp.22.m7). He reads kāma as karman, ‘action’. The Tibetan adds ‘it is dharmatā’ (chos nyid).

flags.note: paramārthavid yogināṃ acintyo hi is read as paramārthavid-yoginām, ‘for yogis who know the ultimate, it is indeed inconceivable’, the masculine acintyaḥ agreeing with an unstated dharmaḥ (the song’s dhāma, ‘that dharma is inconceivable’). Alternative: ‘the knower of the ultimate is indeed inconceivable to yogis’, echoing ‘we are inconceivable yogis’ (cp.22.m3). The Tibetan supports the first: don dam par rig pa'i rnal 'byor pa la bsam du med pa'i phyir chos nyid do, ‘since it is inconceivable for the yogi who knows the ultimate, it is dharmatā’.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ends with chos nyid do, ‘it is dharmatā (the nature of things)’, naming what the song’s dhāma refers to; the Sanskrit comment names nothing. The Tibetan song line has de chos, ‘that dharma’.

Munidatta’s paraphrase uses karman, ‘action’ (janmanā karma, karmaṇā… utpādaḥ), where the song has kāma, which can also mean ‘desire’; the Tibetan has las, ‘action’, in the song and the comment. The draft line already follows this reading (glossary karma).

vartma(tmā)māhātmyam carries Shastri’s parenthesis; either way the sense is ‘the greatness of the path’, which the Tibetan lam gyi bdag nyid kyi che ba confirms (bdag nyid kyi che ba being the regular rendering of māhātmya). pañca[ma]padena has a restored syllable; the closing numeral 22 (the song number) is not translated.

questions: cp.22.m4: sambhavāhavena looks corrupt. I rendered ‘no difference is apprehended between the living person and the dead’, taking ‘the dead’ from the song line and the Tibetan (shi ba). Is that acceptable, or would you rather print the word untranslated with a note, or adopt a conjecture such as saṃbhavābhāvena?

cp.22.m6: the Tibetan has ‘having gained the guru's path’ (bla ma'i lam thob nas) where Munidatta has gurumārgālabdhatvāt, ‘because they have not gained the guru's path’. I followed the Sanskrit and put the difference in the note (cp.22.m6). Should the woven note carry it, or only the flag?

cp.22.m3: the Tibetan has no ‘we do not know’ and seems to read the sentence as ‘“birth and…” means as it is for worldly people’ ('jig rten pa ji lta ba bzhin du gyur pa). I mention this briefly in the note (cp.22.m3); keep or move to the flag only?

cp.22.m7: paramārthavid yogināṃ acintyo hi: I read ‘for yogis who know the ultimate, it is indeed inconceivable’ (with the Tibetan) rather than ‘the knower of the ultimate is inconceivable to yogis’. Do you agree?

cp.22.m2: the Tibetan says people ‘both bind and free themselves’ in existence; Munidatta’s Sanskrit has only binding (cp.22.m2). I put this in the note because it changes the point; is that the right weight?

Munidatta writes Sarahapāda; I used the surface [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha} although the entry’s English is ‘Saraha’, as with Bhusukupāda. Should the honorific form stay in commentary translations, or be reduced to ‘Saraha’?

cp.22.m3: utpādādibhaṅga (‘arising-etc.-perishing’) is rendered ‘arising and so on through perishing’. Would you prefer to supply ‘abiding’ (‘arising, abiding and perishing’), which the verse quoted next names?
cp.22.m1: the note glosses ‘that same meaning’ as ‘presumably that of the preceding song’. Munidatta does not say so (cp.22.m1); keep the hedge or drop it?
